extracted.intended_audience: aspiring English orators, preachers, students, and general readers interested in rhetoric and study habits
extracted.subtask_short: advice on English oratory and study
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on effective public speaking (law, parliament, pulpit, stage) and on sensible habits for learning and authorship, with commentary on when gestures, native texts, and literary practices are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize argument over theatrical gesture in English oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: In contexts such as the bar, parliament, and before judges or representatives, a credible testimony or a cogent argument is more effective than 'laboured gesticulation' or violent bodily action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson argues that 'the arm of an orator has little power' on audiences intent on truth; modulation and contortion cannot substitute for evidence and reason. Examples: judges and members of parliament will not be much affected by rolling eyes, puffing cheeks, spreading arms, stamping, or other ostentatious action. Mechanical persuasion was historically banished from the Areopagus as unworthy before judges whose pleasure is to discover right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve physical action primarily for the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Action (gestures, bodily display) is appropriate on the theatre where its artifice can be justified; elsewhere it is difficult to make action both varied and proper and it tends to become ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the English stage action is plentiful and expected, but transporting theatrical action into other places risks absurdity. Stage action succeeds where art and show are legitimately employed; in other venues truth and nature should limit physical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gesture in preaching sparingly and referentially
rubrics_metrics.description: In the pulpit little action can be proper; gestures should illustrate what is naturally or customarily referred to, and avoid vague or indeterminate motion that can settle into ridiculous habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gesticulation may help to reach 'the ignorant and rude' who respond more to vehemence than to propriety, but preachers should apply action only where it naturally explicates what is spoken (e.g., imitating a motion one describes or laying a hand on the breast to express pity). Repeated vague gestures become habits and quickly seem ludicrous; conversion of sinners is more important than elegance, but propriety should be observed when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt theatrical mannerisms as a substitute for substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitual or exaggerated manual or bodily peculiarities, when not grounded in natural reference or custom, are likely to become ridiculous and undermine authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether in oratory or pulpit, mannerisms that are vague, indeterminate, or merely ostentatious will 'settle into habit' and harm credibility. The advice is to avoid adopting action simply to dazzle; show rather than pantomime truth when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer native-language authors and teachers for most learners
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is more speedily instructed by his own language than by any other; before consulting foreign writers, readers should try domestic authors who can often supply what they need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For readers who read for amusement or for domestic usefulness (not those seeking scholarly eminence), English authors are generally sufficient. Johnson notes the 'riches of the English language' and that many valuable books lie buried at home. This is practical guidance for study choices and curriculum selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: English literature suffices competently for many liberal arts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not one of the liberal arts which may not be competently learned in the English language; poets, theologians, critics, and many scientific and mathematical instructors exist in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson asserts that mathematics, mechanical philosophy, philology, criticism, theology, morality, and political knowledge can be pursued through English authors. This counsels against unnecessary recourse to foreign sources unless one aspires to exceptional scholarly attainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain curiosity and disciplined study against distractions and procrastination
rubrics_metrics.description: The decline of zeal for learning in later life is often due not to the insufficiency of learning but to distractions (duties, pleasures), the postponability of study, and the ease of deferral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because learning 'borrows very little from time or place' it may be indefinitely deferred; to avoid habitual idleness one must resist more sprightly pleasures and the temptation to put off study. Practical implication for writers and students: schedule and resolve to preserve attention for intellectual labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid producing or reading redundant, pompous, or merely compilatory works
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers who dress up obvious or common facts in pompous folios or who repeat what is common to many places needlessly burden students and readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failings to avoid: a traveler recounting well-known sights as if novel, a natural historian describing common productions of a small island as though unique, or a collector labeling everything a curiosity. The writer should aim at selection, regularity of disposition, and genuine contribution rather than accumulation of trivial repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value modest, practical accomplishments over affectation of higher station
rubrics_metrics.description: Misapplied genius and false pretensions (affecting pleasures one cannot enjoy or talking on subjects one has no right to understand) are ridiculous and wasteful of talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson illustrates with Sam Softly: abandoning useful, respectable pursuits to adopt gentlemanly affectations leads to specious idleness and contempt. For writers and characterists: depict authenticity and warn against characters whose pretensions are unsupported by knowledge or temperament; for practitioners: match pursuits to abilities and opportunities.
